verses.translation_literal: Praise Yah! Praise, servants of YHWH; praise the name of YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: Hallelujah! Lift your voices. You who serve the LORD, praise him; praise, and let it ring out. Praise the name of the LORD.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a call to a choir, and it is spoken three times with rising weight: halelu, halelu, halelu. Ibn Ezra reads the triple call as a rhetorical device, the way the temple is named three times in Jeremiah; Radak says it means we owe him many praises. Stage it as three entrances, each a little wider than the last, from the opening cry to the named servants to the name itself.

The KJV's 'Praise ye the LORD' hides that the first line is one word, Hallelujah, with the short divine name Yah inside it, a shout rather than a sentence. 'Servants of the LORD' is not a modest phrase: in the ancient Near East a servant (eved) was a member of a great house with a name and standing in it, as a minister was a servant of the king. The ones being called are those who officiate and live in YHWH's house: priests, Levites, the pilgrims at the gate. KJV 'O ye servants' adds an archaic address not in the Hebrew. 'The name' stands for the whole person, his reputation and presence, and to praise it aloud is to invoke it.

This psalm opens the Egyptian Hallel (Pss 113-118), sung at Passover; the audience would hear Egypt behind every line.

philological_notes.note: Plural imperative of halal, to praise with loud, even boisterous voice; the same root gives 'hallelujah' (halelu + Yah). The root also means 'to boast' and 'to shine'. Ibn Ezra on Ps 113:1 and Radak on Ps 113:1 each explain the threefold repetition.

'Servants of YHWH'. Radak takes them to be the wise and God-fearing; Meiri says they are the surviving sages, and that the command is meant to point away from worship of the host of heaven. The expression is also a title of honour.

verses.translation_literal: May the name of YHWH be blessed from now and until forever.
verses.translation_dramatic: May the name of the LORD be blessed. Blessed now, in this breath, and blessed on and on, past the end of what any of us will see.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood changes. The imperatives of verse 1 give way to a wish, yehi, 'may it be', and the voices turn from the leader's cry to the whole assembly's answer, like an amen. KJV 'Blessed be' is right and YLT's 'is blessed' flattens a prayer into a statement. Malbim sees a distinction here between halal (praise for greatness, which even the nations will give) and barakh (blessing, which acknowledges the constant flow of gifts from a God who is involved in the world); I take that as his reading, but the shift in verb is real.

'From now' (me'attah) is a hard marker: the singers set the moment of the liturgy as the beginning of the blessing, and 'olam, here 'forever', is a long horizon, a time one cannot see to the end of, not abstract eternity. KJV's 'from this time forth and for evermore' is good English but pads three Hebrew words into seven.

philological_notes.note: Pual participle of barakh, 'blessed' or 'to be blessed'; the root's old sense is to kneel and to give or receive favour. With the jussive yehi it makes a wish, not a report. Radak says the blessing is 'in the mouth of the creatures', since all who know are bound to bless him.
A formula meaning 'from now to the distant horizon'. Radak glosses 'now' as the present time and 'olam' as the time to come.

verses.translation_literal: From the rising of the sun to its setting, praised [is] the name of YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: From the place where the sun first breaks over the hills to the place where it sinks away, the name of the LORD is praised, praised from one edge of the day to the other.
verses.directors_commentary:
The sun is the clock and the compass of this verse. 'Rising' and 'going in' are the east and the west, the whole width of the known world measured by a single day's walk of the sun. The verb is the same halal as in verse 1: the opening command is now a fact, or a duty, across the whole world.

The KJV's 'going down of the same' is an old English filler for the Hebrew suffix, 'its'. Ibn Ezra notes that the sun's course gives the length of the inhabited world, twelve hours, not its width. Radak points out that even those who worship stars and planets agree, in the end, that he is the highest cause, and that is the point of the verse: the praise does not stop at Israel's border. Meiri hears an argument here against star-worship. A hearer in an Israel surrounded by sun gods (Shamash, Re) would catch the irony that the sun itself is only a timekeeper in the procession.

In a world without clocks, 'sunrise' and 'sunset' also divide the day into two shifts of work, so the verse promises praise on every shift.

philological_notes.note: 'Rising of the sun', the east. Metzudat Zion glosses it as the place where the sun rises, and 'its setting' (mevo'o, from bo', to enter) as the west.

Pual participle: 'praised', with the sense 'worthy of praise' in the translations that add 'to be'. The Hebrew has no verb 'to be', so the force is open. Metzudat David reads it as the voice of all who live in the east and in the west.

verses.translation_literal: High above all nations [is] YHWH; above the heavens, his glory.
verses.translation_dramatic: High above every nation sits the LORD, and above even the heavens, higher still, his glory.
verses.directors_commentary:
From the width of the earth the psalm goes straight up. The verse is built as a staircase: above the nations, then above the heavens. The second line has no verb, which makes it sound like an exclamation, 'above the heavens, his glory!'. Say it with the voice dropping to a hush, as if no instrument could reach that high.

The KJV reads fine but smooths the structure. The key word is goyim, the 'nations', the peoples with their own gods and their own armies. Meiri reads 'nations' as the gods that the nations serve, the host of heaven, which is why the next clause goes beyond the heavens: the celestial bodies that the neighbours worship are below YHWH, not beside him. This is polemic in one line. Ibn Ezra offers two readings, that he is high above all the praises of the nations, or that the whole verse runs on to the heavens. Metzudat David locates the glory in the dwelling-place of the Presence, in the sky.

'Glory' (kavod) comes from the word for 'heavy': weight, substance, the thing that makes a king a king.

philological_notes.note: 'High', 'exalted', a stative verb or adjective from the root rum, 'to be high'. It begins the verse, which puts the stress on height. The same root returns in the verb yarim in verse 7, so the one who is high lifts the poor.
'His glory', from kaved, heavy. Radak says the heavens and the angels understand his glory better than humans do, and Ibn Ezra that his glory is above the praise of all the nations.

verses.translation_literal: Who [is] like YHWH our God, the one making high to sit,
verses.translation_dramatic: Who is like the LORD, our God? Who else sits so high, enthroned beyond reach?
verses.directors_commentary:
A rhetorical question, and the whole room knows the answer. 'Who is like YHWH' is the old Israelite shout, the one that contains the name Micah (Mi-ka-Yah, 'who is like Yah') and that echoes at the Sea, 'Who is like you among the gods, YHWH?' (Exod 15:11). It is a claim in a world of many gods: no one on the divine council compares.

The next phrase is hard, and the KJV 'who dwelleth on high' smooths it. The Hebrew is a participle, 'the one making high', with a purpose infinitive, 'to sit': he lifts himself up to be seated, he raises his throne. Rashi and Metzudat Zion say that the extra yod on the end of ha-magbihi (like ha-mashpili, mekimi, moshivi) is an ornament of the poem, not a pronoun. Ibn Ezra mentions a view that the verb is intransitive, 'rises', and reports another that it takes the glory as its object, but he reads it plainly. Radak: since verse 4 mentioned the heavens, and some nations take the host of heaven as their gods, the psalm asks which of all those gods is like ours.

The pronoun 'our' matters. This is the people's God, close and not only grand.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil participle with the article, 'the one who makes high'. The final yod is a poetic ending (hireq compaginis); Rashi lists it with the yod in המשפילי, מקימי, להושיבי and מושיבי, and Metzudat Zion says the extra yods are a feature of the holy language. Ibn Ezra reviews whether the verb is intransitive.
'Who is like YHWH?' A question that expects the answer 'no one'. Radak says the point is that of all the gods of the peoples none is like him.

verses.translation_literal: the one making low to see, on the heavens and on the earth?
verses.translation_dramatic: And yet he bends down, he lowers himself to look, at the heavens, and at the earth.
verses.directors_commentary:
The sentence of verse 5 runs on and turns. The same ending, -i, the same article, the same participle, and the opposite direction: high to sit, low to see. The two halves are a matched pair, hamagbihi and hamashpili, like a gesture of rising and then stooping. Let the actor's body do it: the voice climbs in verse 5 and bows in verse 6.

The KJV, 'who humbleth himself to behold the things that are in heaven', adds the words 'himself' and 'the things that are'. In Hebrew he looks 'at the heavens and at the earth', and even the heavens are a long way down. That is the point Metzudat David makes: next to his height even the sky counts for nothing. Ibn Ezra adds that it is knowledge more than condescension: he sees all things, and everything is low before him. Radak, too, reads it as the high one looking down on everything below. Some commentators (Radak mentions them) divide the two verbs between heaven and earth, high in heaven and looking at earth, but the text says he stoops to look at both.

The image is of a king on a raised throne leaning forward to see a petitioner.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil participle of shafel, 'to be low', so 'the one who makes low' (himself or the things he looks at). It may be reflexive, 'who stoops'. Metzudat David reads it as lowering his eyes to watch over everything done in heaven and earth.

verses.translation_literal: Raising from the dust the poor; from the ash heap he lifts the needy,
verses.translation_dramatic: He reaches down and raises the poor man out of the dust. From the ash heap he lifts the beggar, and sets him on his feet.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the sky comes down to the street. The God whose glory is above the heavens looks at the lowest place there is, and moves. Two verbs, qum (raise) and rum (lift), the second the same root as ram, 'high', in verse 4: the high one makes the low high.

The KJV 'dunghill' is accurate to the smell and wrong about the picture. The ashpot was the town's rubbish and ash heap outside the gate, where the burned dung used for fuel and the household's refuse were thrown; the destitute slept and begged on it (compare Job 2:8, where Job sits among the ashes, and Lam 4:5). Metzudat Zion glosses the word as dung and refuse. 'Dust' and 'ash heap' are the two lowest places; the poor man, dal, is thin and without power, and the needy, evyon, is the one who begs. A hearer would see the heap at the town edge, and the hand reaching in.

The lines are a close echo of Hannah's song: 'He raises the poor from the dust, he lifts the needy from the ash heap' (1 Sam 2:8). Malbim reads the verse against the idea that fate is set by the stars: poverty, he says, does not hang on the planets.

philological_notes.note: 'Ash heap', the town rubbish mound. A singular, though it looks plural; Radak and Ibn Ezra say it is a singular noun. Metzudat Zion glosses it as dung and refuse. The root is probably shaphat, to set or place. The same word is in 1 Sam 2:8 and Lam 4:5.

'Poor', literally 'low' or 'hanging', from dalal. Meiri takes the verse to say God repays the good according to their deeds; Malbim says the evyon is worse off than the dal, and the ash heap is lower than the dust.

verses.translation_literal: to make [him] sit with nobles, with the nobles of his people.
verses.translation_dramatic: And he does not stop there. He seats him among the nobles, among the nobles of his own people.
verses.directors_commentary:
Up from the ash heap, and into the best seats. The verse moves from standing to sitting: 'raise', then 'seat'. To sit with someone was to eat at their table and to be counted in their council, and the gate, where elders sat to judge, is the picture behind it. The man who slept on the heap is now at the gate with the ones who decide.

The KJV 'princes' is too royal. The Hebrew nedivim is 'noble, generous people', persons of standing, and the same word means one who gives freely. They are not kings, but the leading men of a clan. The repeated 'with the nobles ... with the nobles of his people' is a doubling for emphasis, and the KJV adds 'even' to smooth it. Malbim sees something in 'his people': a stranger might be honoured by those who do not know him, but here the ones who seat him know exactly where he came from. Radak adds that God's own people are high above the nations when they do his will.

philological_notes.note: 'Nobles'; from the verb nadav, to give willingly. The word joins high rank and open-handedness. Meiri glosses it as 'honoured ones'; Metzudat David says that 'with the nobles of his people' names the best among the nobles.

verses.translation_literal: Making sit the barren woman [in] the house, a mother of the children, joyful. Praise Yah!
verses.translation_dramatic: He settles the childless woman in her house, and makes her a mother, a mother of children, glad. Praise the LORD!
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm that began in the sky ends in a kitchen. After the nobles, the last person God lifts is a woman nobody would have counted: the 'aqarah, the barren wife, who in a household economy had no standing and no security. A woman's place was bought with sons; without them she could be set aside, replaced by a second wife, or left at the mercy of her husband's kin. The line turns on the verb 'sit' again: the same root as 'to sit' in verse 5 and 'to seat' in verse 8. God sits on high, sits the beggar with the nobles, and sits the barren woman in a home.

The KJV 'maketh the barren woman to keep house' reads 'sit' as 'keep house', and is not wrong about the gist, but it hides the verb. Radak and Ibn Ezra say 'aqeret is not in construct with 'house', so the house is where she is seated, as in 'sit in a house'. Radak adds that she is joyful in place of her former grief. The end, 'a mother of children, joyful', has the word order reversed in English: the Hebrew leaves 'joyful' for last, so the line closes on gladness, and then the whole room cries Hallelujah.

The tone recalls Hannah (1 Sam 2:5), Sarah and Rachel. Rashi and the Targum read the barren woman as Zion or the assembly of Israel, and cite Isa 66:8 for the joyful mother.

philological_notes.note: 'The barren woman [in] the house'. Ibn Ezra and Radak read 'aqeret as an absolute form in the pattern of gevirah, not a construct chain. Rashi and Meiri read the barren woman as Zion, the nation as a whole, and Malbim has a household in which one wife drank a cup of barrenness.
The closing 'Hallelujah' matches the opening of verse 1 and frames the psalm. Radak says it is said because of all these wonders; Ibn Ezra says the poet seals the psalm with it for the same reason.
